title: Development of New Aluminium Alloys for Future Automotive Structural Components With Less Criticality and Higher Casting Processability
abstract: Abstract The linear economy follows a “take-make-dispose model, while the circular economy aims for closed-loop system where resources are reused, recycled and regenerated, minimizing waste and environmental impact. Following that, the surge in integration from linear economy to circular economy has been widely witnessed in various European industries for past few years. In automotive industry, aluminium and its alloys are defined as the most suitable candidates, that meets circular economy principles along with technical requirements. However, as per publication by European Commission (EC) on Critical Raw Materials (CRMs), aluminium and its major alloying elements, i.e. silicon and magnesium are declared as CRMs. This poses new constraints to usage of these elements in various automotive structural components. Under these premises, the aim of this work is to implement an innovative roadmap for the development of high-performance aluminium alloys with low content of CRMs and enhanced casting processability. The presented approach shows that by incorporating low criticality concept with high casting processability, it is possible to come up with advanced aluminium alloys with higher mechanical performance that fulfills the requirements of todays manufacturing while addressing global resource challenges. This work also envisioned that researchers in foundry could utilize the descripted approach in designing new aluminium alloys for future applications. Graphic Abstract

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The European Commission (EC) under the frame of European Green Deal is transforming European Union (EU) policies on climate, energy, transportation and other sectors to make first ever climate neutral continent. The aim of this deal is to reduce net greenhouse gases emissions at least 55% by 2030 and eliminate them completely by the end of 2050. 1  Following these stringent policies by EC, the European automotive industry is undergoing radical transformation from internal combustion engines (ICEs) to electric-power driven vehicles. This transition towards electrification not only addresses the change of the propulsion system but also encompasses a complete overhaul in the car design, manufacturing process and material selection. Moreover, with increased public awareness of climate change, the demand for electrical vehicles (EVs) has witnessed a sharp increase in the last few years and European automotive giants like Audi, BMW and others are making significant investments in their R&D to compete in this growing market. 2

One of the major challenges in EV manufacturing is to optimally manage the vehicle weight while achieving the best battery performance. As lightweight vehicles require less energy consumption, therefore extending the battery mileage plays a crucial role in increasing EV sales. While looking for a potential material selection that offers lightweight characteristics and meets clean and green technology goals, aluminium and its alloys are considered as the supreme choice. Aluminium alloys possess light weight characteristics along with other unique properties, i.e. low density, high thermal conductivity, excellent corrosion resistance and good machinability, which make them further ideal for manufacturing various automotive components. 3 ,  4 ,  5 – 6  Because of these versatile properties, aluminium and its alloys are being increasingly used in EVs production and, as a result, the demand for related raw materials has also grown significantly.

Despite the availability of its abundant RMs, i.e. bauxite (primary ore of aluminium), industries are still opting for recycled aluminium for end-use production, as the energy consumption and emission of greenhouse gas are significantly less as compared to that resulting from primary aluminium production. 7  Considering the European aluminium industry’s pivotal role in the transition towards sustainable technologies, bauxite was listed as critical raw material (CRM) in 2020 by EC. 8  In the latest publication, 9  primary and recycled aluminium were assessed together because of their consistency reasons and declared as CRMs. Apart from aluminium, obviously being the main element in aluminium alloys, there are certain alloying elements like silicon and magnesium which play a major role in the production of various structural components have been declared as CRMs since their inclusion in criticality assessment as RMs. 10 ,  11 ,  12 – 13  Therefore, a more climate-friendly approach is required to counter this challenge with the aim of providing mitigating actions against high usage of CRMs in aluminium alloy development.

The report made by Ducker frontier for European Aluminium, 14  shows that the average aluminium content per vehicle in 2019 was 179 Kg, and is expected to increase by 20 Kg, i.e. 199 kg by 2025 with casting to remain the dominant forming process. Among various casting processes, high-pressure die casting (HPDC) has emerged as the essential near-net shape manufacturing process for the production of modern electric vehicle components. Using HPDC, complex shapes with thin wall thickness can be produced, having higher dimensional accuracy at relatively low production costs. However, number of critical parameters associated with HPDC, i.e. high velocity of molten metal at ingates (up to 60 m/s 13 ), high cooling rate (up to ~10 3  K/s 15 ) and high pressure (up to ~120 MPa) makes this process very complex. Moreover, non-synchronization of these parameters is the major source for the formation of inner and surface casting defects.

While designing new alloys for aluminium casting applications, especially in the context of sustainability, it is very crucial to incorporate a range of key indicators to ensure the performance of alloy as well as long term environmental viability. Hence alloy designing process not just target the optimizing the alloy for its mechanical properties, but also consider its life cycle chain, i.e. from extraction to recycling, as well geopolitical and economic impacts of sourcing RMs. The present work is aimed at implementing a strategy presented by the same authors 16  in form of a detailed case study to design new aluminium alloys for the production of future EVs structural components, i.e. shock tower and frontal frame, 2 , 17 , 18  to show the potential of the proposed methodology. The material selection will be performed using the Ashby material selection approach 19  which by date is considered as most acknowledged strategy for choosing potential material for particular engineering applications. The main objective of this work will be to develop new aluminium alloys who have the potential to meet the desired less criticality issues along with high HPDC processability, meanwhile ensuring the design and mechanical requirements of the final component must not be compromised.

sections.heading: Proposed Methodology Implementation Strategy
paragraphs: In the automotive industry, regardless of the type of propulsion system used, shock towers are considered essential passenger safety components. As part of the chassis, this component must absorb high loads in a crash situation. It connects the shock absorber with the front part of the body and disperses all the forces that the shock absorber experiences. The shock towers were commonly manufactured through the sheet metal fabrication process, while frontal frames were primarily composed of several assembled parts to form a framework to support the frontal structure of the vehicle. These components were usually made of steel or thick gravity casting in a typically heavy structure. Considering the gap, there is a huge potential to achieve a reduction in weight if produced by aluminium alloy through HPDC while maintaining the desired requirements. However, both components (shock tower and frontal frame) must not only meet safety requirements but also have to meet stringent mechanical and manufacturing criteria. These components should have excellent castability and high mechanical performance, i.e. high yield strength, fatigue resistance and impact toughness to sustain operational load and crash induced deformations without failure. Therefore selected alloy system must possess superior castability, characterized by high fluidity, lower susceptibility for hot tearing and minimal solidification shrinkage to produce defect free components, particularly in these thin wall casting applications, where rapid heat extraction and constrained flows path increase the risk for misruns and porosity formations. Moreover the alloy must maintain adequate ductility and fracture toughness at reduced thickness section to ensure energy dissipation during impact events. Hence optimal balance between casting processability and mechanical performance is very essential to produce these components. The required mechanical properties for these components are given in Table  1 . sections.heading: Starting Alloying Systems
paragraphs: To start with the development of new aluminium alloys, existing commercial alloys were considered who have the potential to meet the desired mechanical properties of components and on which the proposed methodology 16  can be implemented. Among available choices, Al–Mg and Al–Si families are the most used for manufacturing multiple automotive components because of their high strength-to-weight ratio, good corrosion resistance, high recyclability and most importantly superior mechanical properties. 20 ,  21 ,  22 – 23  From the Al–Mg family, Al–Mg (2,3)  and AlMg 4 Fe 2  alloys have been selected because of their attractive combination of moderate strength, good ductility and high corrosion resistance in as-cast condition. On the side of the Al–Si family, AlSi 10 MnMg alloy has been selected, as the presence of high Si content as a major alloying element promotes excellent castability to generate complex shapes, while Mg (up to 0.4 wt%) as minor alloying content enhances mechanical performance without inhibiting positive characteristics of alloy. The chemical composition and mechanical properties of these selected starting alloy systems are given in Table  2 . However, these alloys have 2 facets: on one hand, they have the potential to meet the desired mechanical performance of components but, on the other hand, they contain a high content of CRMs as alloying elements, i.e. Si and Mg. Considering these alloys as starting alloying systems, the approach towards development of new alloys will include exploring of their real potential and capabilities by : Effectively reducing the CRMs content to their lower limits, i.e. Mg content in the range 2.1–2.7 wt% in Al–Mg (2,3)  and 3.8–4.1 wt% in AlMg 4 Fe 2  alloy; in AlSi 10 MnMg alloys, Si content has been studied in the range from 7.5 to 11.5 wt% and Mg content from 0.15 to 0.35 wt%. Maintaining proper level of mechanical properties by considering cooling rates, grain refinement, formation and strengthening effect provided by alternative addition of non- or low CRM alloying elements related to their added concentration. Reduction of Si and Mg in AlSi 10 MnMg will be associated with heat treatment, as formation of β” precipitates during heat treatment contributes significantly to material strengthening. While for Al–Mg alloys, being non-heat treatable, mechanical properties will be associated with formation of fine grains and solid solution strengthening, i.e. replacing Mg with alternative non- or low CRM alloying elements. Detailed description for mechanical compensation of Si and Mg is given in Section “ Mechanical Compensation of Si and Mg ”. Ensuring high HPDC processability, as there are certain key parameters, i.e. fluidity and solidification shrinkage, which cause the formation of several internal and external casting defects. Microstructural prediction and response by these key characteristics will be made by mean of CALculation of PHAse Diagram (CALPHAD) 24 , 25  (a thermodynamic approach) to allow the evaluation of various alloy features. The strength of the CALPHAD method lies in the fact that it provides efficient calculations in multiphase systems offering the required accuracy necessary for practical applications. The TCAL7 (Al-based thermodynamic) database provided by Thermo-Calc ®  was used for the evaluation in this study. sections.heading: Mechanical Compensation of Si and Mg
paragraphs: Despite the importance of reducing the content of CRMs, such as Si and Mg, it is well known that lower content of Si and Mg in aluminium castings can significantly affect the alloy’s mechanical properties and casting performance. Therefore, mechanical compensation to their reduction is required. While seeking their compensation, various options may be adopted, including: 1) substitution of these elements (Si and Mg) with other non-CRMs or lower-CRM alternatives that provide similar solution strengthening effects, 2) grain refinement and 3) precipitation hardening.

sections.heading: Solid Solution Strengthening
Grain refinement
paragraphs: In general, grain size plays a vital role in achieving a good balance between strength, ductility and toughness of a material. Reducing the grain size, also called grain refinement, is one of the strengthening mechanisms used for cast metal alloys. Finer grains in comparison with coarse grains, offer more grain boundaries, which in turn provide more obstacles for the dislocation motion, hence increasing the strength by Hall-Petch relationship. The grain refinement in casting can be achieved by introducing alloying elements, controlling the cooling rate or through rapid solidification process. Grain refinement can be achieved by alloying with titanium (Ti), boron (B), or zirconium (Zr), which promote the formation of fine grains during solidification. Among these elements, Ti is often used as a grain refiner in aluminium alloys to promote the formation of fine and uniform grains. 28  However, considering the high thermal conductivity of aluminium alloys for thin wall casting and the rapid solidification process characterizing the HPDC process automatically results in producing fine grains and thus no special measures are mandatory for grain refinement while developing new alloys.

sections.heading: Precipitation Hardening
paragraphs: For aluminium castings, different processing solutions can be applied for precipitation hardening through different heat treatment processes such as T4, T5, T6 or T7 as shown in Figure  1 .  For HPDC of AlSiMnMg alloys, the most used heat treatment is direct artificial ageing (T5) or in some cases, a so-called stabilization treatment (at temperature up to 300 °C) is performed on as-cast components. The T6 heat treatment of AlSiMnMg alloys includes solubilization of as-cast component at higher temperature (~ 470–520 °C) for several hours to dissolve  β -Mg 2 Si phase into aluminium matrix, which later forms fine nanoscale  β ” precipitates during ageing process which are highly coherent in the  α -Al matrix and ultimately enhance the mechanical properties. However, considering the peculiarities of HPDC process, when thin and complex shapes are produced, a solid solution treatment at a higher temperature for a longer period of time is usually avoided for diecast parts to minimize the risk of part distortion and surface blistering caused by the air entrapment in the castings. Therefore, the selection of solution time and temperature plays a critical role. These heat treatment solutions can lead to different amounts, size, and distribution of the reinforcement phase Mg 2 Si, which practically means that different combinations of elongation, YS and UTS can be achieved by the treated alloy. The optimization of heat treatment is fundamental to achieve the desired combination of strength and ductility. sections.heading: Designing of SETs and Variants
paragraphs: To design new alloys, starting alloy systems were divided into twelve SETs with varying chemical compositions (wt%) as shown in Table  4 . For each SET, the composition was designed in such a way that reduction in Si and Mg contents is achieved by replacing them with other elements to compensate their effect in terms of reducing CRMs content meanwhile ensuring that the alloy castability must not be compromised. In first two SETs the main goal was the reduction of Mg content. The Mg content was kept low in the range of 2.1–2.7 wt% in SET1 with possible reinforcing action associated with a certain amount of Mn, Zn and Co, while in SET 2, in range of 3.8–4.1 wt% with possible reinforcement associated with Mn, Zn, Cu and Ti. The AlSi 10 MnMg alloy system was divided in 3 categories, i.e. AlSi 10 MnMg0.3 (SET 3, 4, & 5), AlSi 10 MnMg0.2 (SET 6, 7, 8 & 9) and AlSi 8 MnMg0.3 (SET 10, 11, & 12). For SETs 3 to 12, minimization of Si and Mg content was performed with possible reinforcing action associated with Cu, Mn, Zn, Mg and Ti. From each SET, multiple number of variants were designed for criticality and castability assessment. Overall 368 variants (44 for SET1, 54 for SET2 and 27 for each SET from 3 to 12) were investigated. For each variant, criticality index and castability characteristic were evaluated to identify the best viable options. Initially all SETs were evaluated collectively from best to worse on a scale of 1 to 5 (in form of scalebar), with 1 referring to worst while 5 refers to best SET. Once best SETs were found, then best variants among them which reflect the least criticality and high castability properties will be considered for further mechanical investigation. The designed variants, their respective chemical compositions, are given in Appendix. sections.heading: Evaluation of Mechanical Compensation of Silicon and Magnesium Reduction in Designed SETs
paragraphs: The high cooling rate in HPDC results in super saturated solid solution of alloying elements, whose quantification is difficult. However, in design SETs, some elements can play a critical in solid solution strengthening such as Cu, Fe, Mg, Mn and Zn. As summarizes in Table  5  maximum solubility (at binary eutectic composition) is shown by Zn, Mg and Cu. It is reasonable to considered that, when these elements are present in minimum quantity in aluminium alloys, could be in solid solution after HPDC. sections.heading: Criticality Assessment
Castability Assessment
paragraphs: Generally, castability refers to the ability of metal materials to obtain defect free castings. Till date, there is no standard procedure available for defining castability of metals in term of measurable parameters. A survey involving 60 European aluminium foundries has been performed some years ago, offering a broad picture in terms of quality of castings and more frequently detected defects and imperfections, as well as of degree of knowledge and application of CEN standards. 36  Considering the findings, castability assessment of aluminium alloys is heavily dependent upon certain key properties, which includes fluidity, solidification shrinkage, die soldering, sludge formation, hot tearing.
A systematic approach for evaluation of these properties was defined for rapid and comprehensive estimation of castability. 16

Fluidity, being the most essential parameter for producing high integrity castings, was estimated first. The viscosity (considered as inverse of fluidity) was used as reference property to estimate the fluidity of the designed variants. The viscosity calculation for each variant was conducted through an analytical model using CALPHAD approach performed by Thermo-Calc ®  software at a typical HPDC processing temperature of 680 °C. Figure  3 . shows kinematic viscosity for all sets along with their rankings. It can be clearly observed that Al–Mg has much higher viscosity as compared to Al–Si alloy systems. In particular, AlSi 10 MnMg0.3 (SET 3, 4, & 5) and AlSi 10 MnMg0.2 (SET 6, 7, 8 & 9) shows minimum viscosity (i.e. highest fluidity). While looking for best options, variants 19–27 for these SETs shows maximum of fluidity response because of higher Silicon content. Figure 3 Kinematic viscosity at 680 °C of all SETs and their rankings.

The die soldering phenomena is a typical defect in HPDC which occur when molten metal comes in contact with die steel during the filling and solidification stage of the casting process. The molten metal reacts with iron from the die to form hard phases and compounds which act as inclusions to affect the fluidity of molten alloy. The extent of this reaction is mitigated by a relatively high content of Iron and Manganese in the molten alloy, as described in Ref.  37 . Figure  5 37  offers an estimation about die soldering index (DSI) for various AlSi alloys. If Mn content is 0.45 wt%, 0.55 wt% and 0.65 wt% ,  then DSI value range lies in range from 6 to 8, 3 to 5 and 0 to 1, respectively. For alloy systems under investigation, AlSi 10 MnMg0.2 (SET 3,4 & 5) and AlSi 10 MnMg0.3 (SET 6, 7, 8 & 9), considering that Mn content lies in the range of 0.45–0.65 wt % with Fe of 0.2 wt%, an increase in the quantity of Si (from 8 to 10) can be certainly associated with a decrease in DSI. Figure 5 Estimation of Die Soldering Index (DSI) for SET 10, 11 & 12 (yellow boxes highlight possible range of DSI values for the designed variants) elaborated from Ref.  37 .

Figure  6  summarizes Extraction Index values for all SETs along with their rankings. It can be observed that SET 1 & 2 have the highest extraction index, with some favourable cases ranging between 1.2 and 1.8%. Figure 6 Extraction index for all SETs along with their rankings.
Figure  7  presents the sludge fraction (%) for all designed alloys with their ranking. Figure 7 Sludge fraction (%) for all designed variants with their rankings.

It can be observed that SET 1 & 2 present the highest sludge fraction values with some variants showing some favourable cases between 0.5 to 0.8%. SETs 3-7 and 10–12 show the lowest overall value of the sludge fraction with a favourable variant within value ranges between 0 and 0.35%. SET 8 & 9 give high dispersion in values with some favourable variants whose values lie in the range of 0–0.8%.

Hot tearing is the undesired formation of irregular cracks in metal castings, generated during solidification and cooling, typically while the casting is still inside the die cavity. The cause of hot tearing is generally attributed to the development of thermally induced tensile stresses and strains in a casting. It occurs in the final stage of solidification at intrinsic position of the castings, such as inside corners or fillets of casting geometries, where casting shrinkage is constrained by the relatively rigid die cavity. Hot tearing is mainly influenced by alloy chemistry and processing variables. Typically, alloys with a wide thermal freezing range are more susceptible to hot tearing than those with a short freezing range. In particular, the final freezing range, called “Thermal Freezing Range” is of high concern. Literature has suggested to evaluate TFR in temperature intervals of mass solid fraction as (of the order of) 95–99.5%. 43  Using Thermo-Calc ®  software, the overall solidification range and TFR between 95 and 99.5% under non-equilibrium conditions were calculated. Figure  8 a & b summarizes results for hot tearing tendency for the designed variants. It is worth mentioning that from each SET, variants with the highest and lowest thermal freezing range are reported in Figure  8 b and ranking was made according to it. It can be clearly observed that SET 1 shows the most critical behaviour, with relevantly very high risk of hot tearing, while SET 3 & 10 presents the least susceptibility to hot tearing. Figure 8 (a) Difference between Liquidus and Solidus temperature ( °C) and (b) Thermal freezing range in non-equilibrium condition.

To have an overall evaluation and ranking of the sets investigated, a score (1 for worst behaviour, 5 for best) has been attributed to each set and to each property contributing to castability. After this, an individual weightage was assigned to calculate the overall castability score for each set. The total sum of weights was set equal to 1. Considering the complex shape of shock towers and frontal frames, fluidity of alloy should be very essential, so it was given the highest weightage of 0.3. The sludge fraction calculated for all the sets was very low and does not significantly impact on the selection, thus it was given a weightage of 0.1. Solidification shrinkage, die soldering and hot tearing have been considered equally critical for the behaviour of HPDC alloys, thus their weightage was set as 0.2.

Considering the ranking obtained by each set, the individual and overall castability score of investigated sets are presented in (Figure  9 a & b). Figure 9 (a) Individual and (b) overall castability score of all investigated SETs.

sections.heading: Development of Screened Alloys and Their Mechanical Characterization
paragraphs: Consequently, based on screening of alloys through sustainability and property target alloy designing, selected variants (as reported in Table  9 ) were casted through HPDC and tensile test were performed at room temperature to determine their mechanical properties, according to the procedure developed by the authors in previous research. 44 , 45  An electromechanical MTS criterion series 40 tensile testing machine equipped with a load cell of 50 kN was used to investigate the tensile properties, according to ISO 6892-1:2019 standard. The extensometer of 25 mm gauge length was applied for strain measurement during tensile testing. Tensile testing was conducted 5 times for each condition at a strain rate of 1 mm/min to ensure repeatability. The targeted composition range of selected alloys is given in Table  10 . Three alloys from Al–Mg alloy family were selected because of low criticality index and to have better behaviour in term of solidification and four alloys from AlSi 8 MnMg alloy family were selected. The ingots for selected alloys were supplied by Raffmetal Spa (Casto, Italy) while the castings were produced by a 2.9 MN locking force cold-chamber HPDC machine. The machine was equipped with dynamic shot control system and plunger velocity; time and pressure were monitored during the entire casting cycle. Firstly, the ingots were melted at 780 ± 10 °C, then the temperature of molten metal was gradually decreased up to (710 ± 5) °C. After, the molten metal was degassed using Argon for 15 minutes along with manual skimming with coated paddle. The nominal plunger velocity was 0.2 m/s in first phase, while during the filling phase, it was equal to 2.7 m/s. The pressure of 40MPa was applied to ensure high integrity castings. The die, made of X38CrMoV5-1 tool steel, was preheated at 230° °C using hot oil circulation to stabilize the temperature. The initial 20 castings were scrapped to reach the quasi-steady-state temperature in shot chamber and die. A 3D representation of the multiple cavity die used to produce HPDC is reported in Figure  11 a. The weight of HPDC specimens were measured ~ 0.9 kg including the runners, biscuit and overflows. The achieved mechanical properties reported are summarized in Figure  11 b. The discussion of the mechanical properties and tensile behaviour will be object of future publications. In all cases, yield strength and elongation requirement for shock tower were achieved and required mechanical strength and elongation for the frontal frame can be achieved by artificial ageing treatment. The literature 30 , 46  has suggested a potential increase of 40–50 MPa in Alloy 4,5,6 and 7 by mean of T5 heat treatment because of presence of Si and Mg content, which results in fine scale nano-precipitation during artificial ageing process to provide the strengthening mechanism, which is focus of future research by the authors. sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The need of innovative strategies in designing alloy composition is made evident by the high number of constrains involved for the development of lightweight automotive components. A specific strategy, considering minimization of critical raw materials usage, good processability characteristics and achievement of required mechanical and technological requirements has been recently elaborated 16  and, in this paper, has been implemented for the definition of optimal aluminium alloys for high-pressure diecast shock towers and frontal frame. The full selection process, based on 12 main sets of variants (for a total of 368 variants), has been presented and the most interesting options have been individuated. 7 selected composition ranges were selected for experimental campaign on lab scale HPDC. Tensile testing shows that in all selected alloys, the yield strength and elongation requirements were achieved for shock tower and potential increase in strength and elongation for frontal frame can be achieved by T5 heat treatment of AlSi 8 MnMg alloys because of formation of  β ” Mg 2 Si nanoscale precipitates during artificial ageing stage.

Further activities are in progress to evaluate their response to heat treatments, move to industrial demonstrators, validate design procedure and designed alloys with respect to current industrial benchmarks.
